questions.prompt: An eligible licensed tenant will pilot password reset with members of the ResetPilot security group. Other ordinary users must remain outside the pilot. Which scope should you select?

options.text: Selected, with ResetPilot as the group
options.explanation: Selected limits ordinary-user SSPR eligibility to the specified security group.

options.text: All
options.explanation: All includes ordinary users throughout the tenant, exceeding the pilot scope.

options.text: None
options.explanation: None disables ordinary-user SSPR, including the intended pilot members.

options.text: Company branding
options.explanation: Branding changes the sign-in appearance; it does not select the users eligible for SSPR.

questions.prompt: A user wants an email alert if someone unexpectedly resets their password through SSPR. Which setting addresses this concern?

options.text: Notify admins when other admins reset passwords
options.explanation: That notification concerns administrator resets rather than notifying this ordinary user.

options.text: Notify users on password resets
options.explanation: This sends reset notifications to the affected user so an unexpected reset can be noticed.

options.text: Require registration at sign-in
options.explanation: Registration gathers recovery information; it does not replace reset-event notifications.

options.text: Change the page background color
options.explanation: Branding changes presentation, not notification of a password-reset event.

questions.prompt: The ordinary-user pilot requires one authentication method. An administrator account instead encounters a two-method reset process. How should you test the ordinary-user experience?

options.text: Lower the administrator reset requirement to one method
options.explanation: The ordinary-user method count does not lower the strong administrator reset requirement.

options.text: Give the test account an administrator role
options.explanation: Adding an administrator role tests the stronger administrator policy rather than the ordinary-user experience.

options.text: Use a licensed non-administrator account in the pilot group
options.explanation: The exercise uses a non-administrator because administrator reset policy has stronger requirements.

options.text: Test only with the administrator already signed in
options.explanation: An existing administrator session can select the wrong account and does not prove the pilot user can reset a forgotten password.

questions.prompt: A synchronized employee needs a cloud password reset to update the password in on-premises Active Directory too. Which design meets this requirement?

options.text: Cloud-only SSPR without writeback
options.explanation: A cloud-only reset does not provide the required writeback to the on-premises directory.

options.text: A custom sign-in background image
options.explanation: Branding does not synchronize passwords or enable writeback.

options.text: An email notification after reset
options.explanation: A notification reports the event; it does not update the on-premises password.

options.text: Supported password writeback with eligible licensing and synchronization
options.explanation: Writeback sends cloud password changes to on-premises AD through supported synchronization; the feature needs eligible licensing.

questions.prompt: You are updating SSPR in a tenant that uses the centralized authentication policy. Where should you manage allowed authentication methods such as Email OTP?

options.text: Authentication methods policy
options.explanation: The centralized policy controls supported authentication methods for authentication and SSPR; security questions remain an SSPR-policy exception.

options.text: Company branding
options.explanation: Company branding controls sign-in presentation rather than permitted recovery methods.

options.text: The custom helpdesk email field
options.explanation: That field supplies a support contact and does not enable Email OTP.

options.text: Only the old SSPR authentication-method checkboxes
options.explanation: After policy migration, supported methods are managed centrally; the old settings are not the correct place for Email OTP.

questions.prompt: The tenant has suitable licensing and a branding administrator. The team wants its logo and background on the sign-in experience. What should it configure?

options.text: A larger SSPR authentication-method count
options.explanation: Method count changes identity verification requirements, not the sign-in appearance.

options.text: Company branding in the intended Entra tenant
options.explanation: Company branding provides the logo, background and other sign-in appearance settings; the exercise then tests the result with a user.

options.text: A custom helpdesk email address only
options.explanation: A helpdesk address supplies support information but does not upload the company logo or background.

options.text: Password writeback
options.explanation: Writeback synchronizes password changes to on-premises AD rather than changing sign-in appearance.

questions.prompt: A workload subnet uses 10.24.8.0/27. How many IPv4 addresses remain assignable to Azure resources after the reserved addresses?

options.explanation: 32 is the total address count before subtracting the five Azure reservations.
A /27 contains 32 addresses. Azure reserves five, leaving 27 assignable addresses.
Subtracting only network and broadcast addresses misses the additional Azure-reserved addresses.
Azure reserves five addresses, not three; 32 minus five is 27.

questions.prompt: A virtual network uses 10.24.0.0/16 and already has a subnet 10.24.8.0/24. Which additional subnet is valid without overlapping that subnet?

options.explanation: This range lies inside the existing 10.24.8.0/24 subnet, so it overlaps.
This range is outside the virtual network address space.
This range is inside 10.24.0.0/16 and does not overlap 10.24.8.0/24.
This range is contained in the existing subnet and therefore overlaps it.

questions.prompt: An on-premises application reaches an Azure VM across an already configured site-to-site VPN. Which VM address supports that private connection?

options.text: Only a public IP address
options.explanation: A public address is not required to reach the VM privately through the VPN.

options.text: The final reserved address in the subnet
options.explanation: The final IPv4 address is reserved by Azure and cannot be assigned to the VM.

options.text: An unused address outside the VM subnet
options.explanation: The VM private IP must come from its deployed subnet, not an unrelated range.

options.text: The private IP address from its subnet
options.explanation: Private addresses support communication inside the virtual network and over configured private hybrid connections.

questions.prompt: A VM must keep a predictable private address for an IP-based firewall rule. An unused, unreserved address is available in its subnet. Which allocation should you configure?

options.text: Static private IP assignment on the NIC IP configuration
options.explanation: Static assignment lets you select the available subnet address and suits a firewall rule that needs a predictable IP.

options.text: Dynamic private IP assignment because it guarantees a chosen address
options.explanation: Dynamic assignment lets Azure select an available address rather than guaranteeing the address you choose.

options.text: Static assignment of an address reserved by Azure
options.explanation: Static allocation still cannot use reserved subnet addresses.

options.text: Add the desired private address to a public IP resource
options.explanation: Private VM addresses are configured on the NIC; a public IP resource does not allocate that private subnet address.

questions.prompt: A Standard public IP resource has been created for a new VM. When is its static public address normally released?

options.text: Whenever the VM is stopped
options.explanation: Stopping the associated VM does not release a static public IP resource.

options.text: When the public IP resource is deleted
options.explanation: Static public IPs are allocated at creation and released when the public IP resource is deleted.

options.text: Whenever the public IP is disassociated from the NIC
options.explanation: Disassociation does not delete the public IP resource or release its static address.

options.text: After its first inbound connection
options.explanation: Receiving traffic does not end the allocation; resource deletion releases it.

questions.prompt: Two workload subnets share a virtual network. Their traffic must pass through a network virtual appliance instead of taking the default subnet-to-subnet path. What is needed?

options.text: Only create the two subnets
options.explanation: Separate subnets alone do not replace the default direct routing between them.

options.text: Assign public IPs to all workload VMs
options.explanation: Public IP assignment does not force private subnet traffic through an appliance.

options.text: Custom routing through the appliance
options.explanation: Azure routes between subnets by default. Custom routes can direct that traffic through the NVA.

options.text: Use overlapping address ranges for the subnets
options.explanation: Overlapping subnet ranges are invalid and do not implement inspection routing.

questions.prompt: An inbound connection is allowed by the subnet NSG but denied by the NIC NSG. Assume no security-admin override applies. What happens?

options.text: The connection is allowed because the subnet is evaluated first
options.explanation: Evaluation order does not make the first scope authoritative; the NIC NSG still filters the connection.

options.text: The connection is allowed if the subnet rule has the smaller priority number
options.explanation: Priorities order rules within an NSG, not allow one NSG to override another.

options.text: The connection is denied
options.explanation: Both applicable NSGs must permit the flow. The subnet allow cannot cancel the NIC deny.

options.text: Azure removes the NIC deny rule automatically
options.explanation: Azure evaluates independently configured NSGs; it does not remove a rule to resolve differing results.

questions.prompt: An NSG has a broad inbound deny at priority 300. You need to allow HTTPS from 198.51.100.24/32 before that deny. Which priority is suitable for the new allow rule?

options.explanation: 310 is evaluated after the matching deny at 300, so it cannot provide the exception.
4096 is valid but runs after the matching priority-300 deny.
50 is outside the custom NSG priority range of 100 to 4096.
240 is within the custom range and is evaluated before 300, allowing a matching HTTPS exception.

questions.prompt: Web-server VMs are added and removed regularly. You want NSG rules to refer to their application role rather than maintain a list of their IPs. What should you use?

options.text: An application security group containing the web NICs
options.explanation: ASGs group VM network interfaces by application role and can be used as NSG sources or destinations.

options.text: The AzureLoadBalancer service tag
options.explanation: That Microsoft-managed tag represents load-balancer probe traffic, not your changing collection of web VMs.

options.text: A DNS CNAME record
options.explanation: A DNS alias does not group NICs for use in an NSG rule.

options.text: A route-table next hop
options.explanation: A next hop controls traffic routing, not application-role membership in a filtering rule.

questions.prompt: A newly created NSG has no custom rules. Considering only NSG filtering, what happens to an outbound connection to a public internet address?

options.text: The final deny always blocks it
options.explanation: The internet allow rule is evaluated before the default final outbound deny.

options.text: The default AllowInternetOutbound rule permits it
options.explanation: Default outbound rules allow internet traffic before the final deny rule. Actual connectivity still needs a valid route and outbound mechanism.

options.text: It requires the inbound AzureLoadBalancer rule
options.explanation: The AzureLoadBalancer inbound rule is unrelated to allowing this outbound internet flow.

options.text: Default NSG rules exist only for inbound traffic
options.explanation: Azure creates both inbound and outbound default rules.

questions.prompt: You need to identify the security rule allowing or denying a proposed TCP flow to a VM, without sending application traffic. Which tool best matches this task?

options.text: A DNS zone alias record
options.explanation: A DNS alias resolves a resource name; it does not evaluate packet filtering.

options.text: A storage replication policy
options.explanation: Storage replication copies blobs and does not diagnose VM NSG rules.

options.text: Network Watcher IP flow verify
options.explanation: IP flow verify evaluates a proposed flow against applicable security rules and reports the allowing or denying rule.

options.text: A public IP resource overview alone
options.explanation: Public IP allocation details do not identify the applicable security rule for the proposed flow.

questions.prompt: A subnet already has an NSG. You need another rule to protect resources in that subnet. Which configuration is valid?

options.text: Attach a second NSG to the same subnet
options.explanation: The subnet association limit is one NSG, so two concurrent subnet NSGs are not valid.

options.text: Attach one NSG per address range in the subnet
options.explanation: The NSG limit applies to the subnet, not separately to its address ranges.

options.text: Delete every default rule before adding the custom rule
options.explanation: Default NSG rules cannot be deleted; higher-priority custom rules can override their effect.

options.text: Add the rule to the existing subnet NSG
options.explanation: A subnet can have at most one associated NSG, and an NSG can contain multiple rules.

questions.prompt: Your registered domain has a public Azure DNS zone, but ordinary internet queries still use the old DNS provider. What change delegates the domain to Azure DNS?

options.text: Add a private virtual-network link
options.explanation: A private-zone link affects private name resolution, not public registrar delegation.

options.text: Change only the website A record at the old provider
options.explanation: That changes a record at the existing provider but does not delegate authority to Azure DNS.

options.text: Create the same public zone again
options.explanation: Creating another Azure zone does not update the domain registrar delegation.

options.text: Replace the registrar name-server delegation with all four Azure DNS name servers
options.explanation: The registrar delegation points resolvers to the authoritative provider; Azure DNS requires all four assigned name servers.

questions.prompt: The name api.example.org should resolve to two IPv4 addresses. How should you represent these in Azure DNS?

options.text: One A record set for api containing both addresses
options.explanation: A record sets group records with the same name and type, so this set can contain both IPv4 addresses.

options.text: One CNAME record set containing both IP addresses
options.explanation: CNAME records contain a target name rather than IPv4 addresses, and a CNAME set has one record.

options.text: One MX record set containing both IP addresses
options.explanation: MX records identify mail-exchange targets; they do not provide the requested IPv4 host mapping.

options.text: Two SOA records for api
options.explanation: SOA records describe zone authority and do not implement the host mapping; an SOA set contains one record.

questions.prompt: The root name example.org must point to a load balancer whose frontend uses a supported Standard public IP resource. Which record avoids hard-coding the address?

options.text: A conventional CNAME at the apex
options.explanation: A conventional CNAME cannot coexist with the apex NS and SOA records and is not allowed there.

options.text: An apex A alias record referencing the public IP resource
options.explanation: An Azure alias can reference the public IP resource from an apex A record, coupling resolution to the resource.

options.text: An MX record referencing the load balancer
options.explanation: MX is for mail routing, not apex IPv4 resolution to a load balancer.

options.text: A TXT record containing the public IP string
options.explanation: TXT data does not provide the A-record address answer clients need.

questions.prompt: Two Azure virtual networks must resolve internal names in the same private DNS zone, without publishing those names publicly. What should you configure?

options.text: Only a registrar delegation for the private zone
options.explanation: Private DNS zones are not exposed through public registrar delegation.

options.text: Public A records for every internal name
options.explanation: Public records publish the internal names, contrary to the requirement.

options.text: A virtual-network link from the private zone to each network
options.explanation: Links let the specified virtual networks resolve the private-zone records without public publication.

options.text: One unlinked private zone and no network links
options.explanation: Creating the private zone alone does not give the networks the required linked-zone resolution.

questions.prompt: An A record had a one-hour TTL when a resolver cached it. You change its address five minutes later. Why might that resolver still return the old address?

options.text: An A record can never be updated
options.explanation: A records can be updated; the apparent delay can be due to cached data.

options.text: The record automatically became a CNAME
options.explanation: Updating an A-record address does not convert it to a CNAME.

options.text: Private-network peering controls the public record TTL
options.explanation: Peering controls network connectivity and does not determine a public DNS record caching lifetime.

options.text: Its cached answer can remain valid until the original TTL expires
options.explanation: TTL controls the caching lifetime, so an already cached answer can remain until its existing expiry.

questions.prompt: You created a www A record in a test public zone, but the test domain is not registered or delegated. How can you verify Azure DNS serves the configured record?

options.text: Query www directly against one assigned Azure DNS name server
options.explanation: An explicit authoritative-server query can inspect the zone record even without public delegation.

options.text: Expect an ordinary recursive lookup to discover the undelegated zone
options.explanation: Without delegation, ordinary resolution has no reason to use that Azure zone.

options.text: Create a private DNS link and claim that proves public delegation
options.explanation: Private linked-zone resolution does not establish public registrar delegation.

options.text: Browse the web server IP and claim that proves the DNS record
options.explanation: Direct IP browsing tests the server, not whether Azure DNS serves the www record.

questions.prompt: Two virtual networks in different supported Azure public-cloud regions need direct private connectivity. Their address spaces do not overlap. Which feature matches this requirement?

options.text: Global virtual network peering
options.explanation: Global peering connects virtual networks in different regions using the Microsoft backbone.

options.text: Regional peering only
options.explanation: Regional peering is the same-region form and does not describe this cross-region connection.

options.text: An Azure DNS A record alone
options.explanation: DNS resolves names but does not establish network connectivity between the two VNets.

options.text: A public IP on each VM as the private link
options.explanation: Public addresses do not create the requested private VNet-to-VNet peering connection.

questions.prompt: Two VNets both use 10.60.0.0/16 and currently cannot be peered. What address-planning change is required before ordinary peering can connect them?

options.text: Add identical DNS servers to both VNets
options.explanation: DNS-server settings do not remove the overlapping IP ranges.

options.text: Give the connected VNets nonoverlapping address spaces
options.explanation: Peered VNet address spaces must not overlap; duplicating the same /16 violates that requirement.

options.text: Create matching NSGs
options.explanation: Security-group configuration does not satisfy the nonoverlapping address-space requirement.

options.text: Select global instead of regional peering to permit overlap
options.explanation: Global peering also requires nonoverlapping address spaces.

questions.prompt: VNet A is peered with hub B, and B is peered with VNet C. No other connectivity or forwarding is configured. What should you expect between A and C?

options.text: Automatic A-to-C transit through B
options.explanation: Two peering relationships do not automatically create transit between the outer VNets.

options.text: A, B and C become one Azure resource
options.explanation: Peered VNets remain separately managed resources and are not merged.

options.text: No automatic A-to-C connectivity through those peerings
options.explanation: Ordinary VNet peering is nontransitive; explicit additional connectivity or routing is needed.

options.text: Global peering would make this same topology transitive
options.explanation: Global peering also does not automatically provide transitive connectivity.

questions.prompt: A hub has a supported VPN gateway. A peered spoke has no gateway and needs to share the hub connection to on-premises networks. Which settings enable gateway transit?

options.text: Use the remote gateway on the hub and allow transit on the spoke
options.explanation: Those settings reverse which network hosts and shares the gateway.

options.text: Deploy a spoke gateway while also selecting the remote gateway
options.explanation: A spoke using a remote gateway cannot also have its own gateway.

options.text: Configure DNS links only
options.explanation: DNS-zone links do not configure VPN gateway sharing or on-premises connectivity.

options.text: Allow gateway transit on the hub and use the remote gateway on the spoke
options.explanation: The hub permits gateway sharing and the spoke selects the remote gateway; the spoke must not have its own gateway.

questions.prompt: You create a peering from VNet A to VNet B. A reports Initiated and no return relationship exists. What remains to establish ordinary two-way peering?

options.text: Create the reciprocal peering and verify Connected on both sides
options.explanation: A complete peering requires relationships in both directions with Connected status on both VNets.

options.text: Treat Initiated as a fully established connection
options.explanation: Initiated indicates the peering is not yet Connected on both sides.

options.text: Delete all subnet NSGs
options.explanation: NSG deletion does not create the missing reciprocal peering relationship.

options.text: Add a public DNS zone
options.explanation: DNS hosting does not complete the VNet peering relationships.

questions.prompt: VMs can communicate by private IP across a peering, but their Azure-provided VM names do not resolve across the two VNets. What should you add for cross-network naming?

options.text: A second identical peering in the same direction
options.explanation: An extra peering does not expand the Azure-provided DNS resolution boundary.

options.text: A suitable linked private DNS zone or custom DNS
options.explanation: Azure-provided name resolution does not automatically span peerings; private linked zones or custom DNS can provide cross-VNet naming.

options.text: A public IP on every VM
options.explanation: Public IPs do not make Azure-provided private VM names resolve across peered networks.

options.text: Remove the remote VNet address space
options.explanation: Removing its address space breaks the network design rather than providing DNS resolution.

questions.prompt: One route table contains UDRs for 10.72.0.0/16 via appliance A and 10.72.5.0/24 via appliance B. Which next hop applies to destination 10.72.5.20?

options.text: Appliance A through the /16 route
options.explanation: The /16 matches but is less specific than the /24.

options.text: Appliance B through the /24 route
options.explanation: Both UDRs match, and the /24 is the longer, more specific prefix.

options.text: Whichever route was created first
options.explanation: Creation order does not replace longest-prefix matching.

options.text: Both appliances receive a copy of every packet
options.explanation: Route selection chooses a next hop rather than duplicating traffic across matching UDRs.

questions.prompt: For an on-premises destination prefix, the effective table contains a UDR and a BGP route with the same prefix. Neither is a service-endpoint route. Which type normally wins?

options.text: The BGP route because it is learned dynamically
options.explanation: Dynamic learning does not give BGP preference over an equal-prefix UDR.

options.text: The older route regardless of type
options.explanation: Creation age is not the documented preference rule.

options.text: The user-defined route
options.explanation: With the same prefix, a UDR normally has higher preference than a BGP route.

options.text: Both routes are always used equally
options.explanation: The documented type preference chooses the UDR rather than automatically sharing traffic.

questions.prompt: A UDR matches the target address and has next-hop type None. No more specific route applies. What happens to matching traffic?

options.text: Azure sends it to the internet
options.explanation: Internet is a different next-hop type; None does not mean use the internet.

options.text: Azure chooses any NVA automatically
options.explanation: An appliance next hop must be configured; None does not select one.

options.text: Azure ignores the route because its next hop is empty
options.explanation: None is an explicit supported drop action, not an incomplete route.

options.text: Azure drops the traffic
options.explanation: The None next hop means matching traffic is dropped rather than forwarded.

questions.prompt: A UDR correctly directs traffic to an Ubuntu NVA. Its Azure NIC has IP forwarding enabled, but guest operating-system forwarding is disabled. What should you do?

options.text: Enable IP forwarding in the guest operating system too
options.explanation: The exercise enables forwarding on both the Azure NIC and inside the guest; both are needed for this NVA forwarding path.

options.text: Only assign a public IP to the NVA
options.explanation: A public IP does not enable the guest to forward packets between workloads.

options.text: Disable IP forwarding on the NIC
options.explanation: The Azure NIC must also allow forwarded traffic, so disabling it makes the design less functional.

options.text: Change the next hop from Virtual appliance to None
options.explanation: None drops matching traffic rather than forwarding it through the NVA.

questions.prompt: The front-end subnet has a route through an NVA to the back-end subnet. The back-end subnet has only system routes. Why can return traffic bypass the NVA?

options.text: UDRs automatically apply to every subnet in the VNet
options.explanation: A table is effective on associated subnets, not automatically on every subnet.

options.text: The forward UDR does not automatically configure the reverse path
options.explanation: A route table affects its associated source subnet. The other subnet needs its own routing if its traffic must also use the appliance.

options.text: Every NVA rewrites all Azure route tables
options.explanation: An NVA does not automatically install the matching reverse UDR in all source subnets.

options.text: System routes cannot send traffic between subnets
options.explanation: Azure system routes provide default communication between subnets in a VNet.

questions.prompt: Three subnets should use the same UDR policy. What route-table association is supported?

options.text: Associate two route tables with each subnet and merge their routes
options.explanation: A subnet cannot have two associated route tables whose routes are merged.

options.text: Attach the route table only to the NSG
options.explanation: Route tables associate with subnets, not with NSGs.

options.text: Associate one route table with all three subnets
options.explanation: A route table can be associated with multiple subnets, while each subnet can have one associated route table.

options.text: Create one route table for every NIC because subnet association is unsupported
options.explanation: Azure supports route-table association at subnet scope; a separate NIC route table is not the association model.

questions.prompt: An application tier must be reached through a private frontend from Azure VMs and an existing on-premises VPN. Which Azure Load Balancer type fits?

options.text: A public load balancer because VPN clients require public addressing
options.explanation: VPN-connected clients can reach a private frontend; this requirement does not call for a public one.

options.text: A DNS TXT record instead of a frontend
options.explanation: A TXT record does not provide load balancing or a private listener.

options.text: An internal load balancer
options.explanation: An internal load balancer uses a private frontend and can serve private Azure and suitably connected on-premises clients.

options.text: An outbound rule without any frontend or load-balancing rule
options.explanation: Outbound SNAT does not configure the requested inbound application-tier service.

questions.prompt: A regional web service must route /images/* and /orders/* to different backend pools and needs WAF protection. Which service better fits than Azure Load Balancer?

options.text: Azure Load Balancer alone
options.explanation: Load Balancer operates at Layer 4 and cannot make the required URL-path decisions or supply a web application firewall.

options.text: Traffic Manager alone
options.explanation: Traffic Manager distributes using DNS; it does not inspect individual URL paths or provide this regional WAF gateway.

options.text: An NSG alone
options.explanation: An NSG filters network traffic using its rules, not HTTP URL paths, and does not act as a WAF gateway.

options.text: Application Gateway with WAF
options.explanation: Application Gateway supports regional Layer 7 path routing and WAF. Azure Load Balancer does not inspect URL paths.

questions.prompt: An HTTP health probe on a Standard Load Balancer receives status 503 from one backend repeatedly until it is marked unhealthy. What happens to new connections for that backend?

options.text: The load balancer stops sending new connections to it
options.explanation: HTTP probes expect status 200. Once the backend is unhealthy, new connections are not directed to it.

options.text: The backend remains healthy because it returned any HTTP response
options.explanation: An arbitrary HTTP response is insufficient; 503 does not satisfy the probe success requirement.

options.text: The load balancer automatically repairs the application
options.explanation: A health probe detects health and affects distribution; it does not repair the backend application.

options.text: All healthy backends are immediately removed from the pool
options.explanation: A failure on this backend does not by itself make the other healthy backends ineligible.

questions.prompt: You want successive connections from the same client IP to prefer the same healthy backend while pool membership remains stable. Which setting addresses this?

options.text: Only the default five-tuple distribution
options.explanation: The default hash includes ports, so successive connections with different source ports need not select the same backend.

options.text: Client IP session persistence
options.explanation: Client IP affinity uses a reduced hash to associate connections from the same client IP with the same backend under the stated stable conditions.

options.text: Only an HTTP health probe
options.explanation: A probe controls backend health eligibility, not client-IP affinity.

options.text: Only an outbound SNAT rule
options.explanation: Outbound rules manage outbound address translation rather than inbound session persistence.

questions.prompt: An administrator needs separate frontend ports on a load balancer to reach individual backend VMs for management. Which feature maps those ports to particular instances?

options.text: An ordinary load-balancing rule across the whole pool
options.explanation: An ordinary rule distributes flows to eligible pool members rather than defining this instance-specific management mapping.

options.text: An outbound rule
options.explanation: Outbound rules configure SNAT for traffic leaving the backend, not inbound instance-specific port mapping.

options.text: Inbound NAT rules
options.explanation: Inbound NAT rules map frontend ports to specific backend instances, matching instance-specific management access.

options.text: A health probe
options.explanation: A probe determines health but does not define the administrator port mapping.

questions.prompt: Backend VMs on a Standard public load balancer need explicitly configured SNAT for connections to public endpoints. Which feature configures this?

options.text: An inbound NAT rule
options.explanation: Inbound NAT maps incoming frontend ports to backend instances, not the requested outbound SNAT policy.

options.text: An HA ports rule on an internal load balancer
options.explanation: HA ports load-balance TCP and UDP flows across all ports for an internal Standard frontend; they do not configure this public outbound SNAT policy.

options.text: Only an HTTP health probe
options.explanation: A health probe determines backend eligibility and does not configure outbound address translation.

options.text: An outbound rule
options.explanation: Outbound rules configure SNAT for the backend pool to communicate with internet or other public endpoints.
